$comment: Phase 13 evaluation labels, written 2026-10-27 together with fixtures/phase13/eval-app, BEFORE any Phase 13 scoring and before any CommitRift command was run on this application. Author: an AI assistant (Claude) working independently of the Phase 13 implementation: it did not read the in-progress Phase 13 Rust changes, it read only the Phase 12 documents and fixtures. No independent human review performed. A label says whether the entry, under the stated environment, can violate the stated property according to PostgreSQL semantics (READ COMMITTED unless stated); `class` is the hazard family a correct discovery should report; `effectful` whether extraction should bind at least one database write; `tables` the tables the entry touches; `pairedWith` (when present) the entry the labeled one runs concurrently with (otherwise two invocations of the entry itself); `observable` (when present) says the property is about what callers are told (return value / response), not about table contents; `replicas` (when present) describes the read-replica routing the label depends on. Labels are frozen (fixtures/phase13/FROZEN.json): do not edit them to improve metrics; corrections go into `corrections` with a reason.

foreignKeys.$comment: SQL names; every foreign key is ON DELETE NO ACTION, ON UPDATE NO ACTION, NOT DEFERRABLE. bookmarks.post_id, comments.author_id, notifications.user_id and folders.parent_id are plain columns.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one team per owner (declared one-team-per-owner)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same owner, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: SELECT the owner's team through the repository, then INSERT; teams.owner_id has no unique constraint. Both INSERTs take FOR KEY SHARE on the owner row for the foreign-key check, which do not conflict with each other.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one team per owner (declared)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same owner, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the owner row serializes the two transactions; the second one's check runs after the first committed and, under READ COMMITTED, its new statement snapshot sees the first team. (Not under REPEATABLE READ: the second transaction's snapshot is taken by its blocked FOR UPDATE statement, before the first commit, so its check misses the first team and it inserts a second one; that environment is not the labeled one.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one team per owner (declared)
cases.environment: createTeam concurrent with createTeamLocked for the same owner, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The Phase 12 foreign-key divergence pattern. createTeam takes no lock for its check. If it checks before createTeamLocked inserts, both insert. On some of these schedules createTeam's INSERT waits: its foreign-key check takes FOR KEY SHARE on the owner row, which conflicts with the FOR UPDATE that createTeamLocked holds. After createTeamLocked commits, the INSERT goes ahead and creates the second team. The violation also happens on a schedule with no wait (createTeamLocked commits before createTeam inserts).

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one team per owner (declared)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same owner, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: SELECT ... FOR SHARE does not conflict with another FOR SHARE. The FOR KEY SHARE lock of each INSERT's foreign-key check does not conflict with FOR SHARE either. Both transactions pass the check and both insert.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: every call completes without a deadlock error (SQLSTATE 40P01)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls adding two different users to the same team (any isolation level)
cases.why: Each INSERT into team_members takes FOR KEY SHARE on the team row (foreign-key check), and the two locks are compatible. Each transaction then asks for FOR UPDATE on the same team row, which conflicts with the other transaction's FOR KEY SHARE. Both wait for each other and the deadlock detector aborts one with 40P01.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: every call completes without a deadlock error, and member_count equals the number of members added
cases.environment: two concurrent calls adding two different users to the same team, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The UPDATE changes only member_count, which is in no unique index, so it takes FOR NO KEY UPDATE. That does not conflict with the other transaction's FOR KEY SHARE. The second UPDATE waits only for the first UPDATE (one direction, no cycle), and under READ COMMITTED it re-reads the committed count and increments it. (Under REPEATABLE READ the second UPDATE fails with 40001 instead; that is not the labeled environment.)

cases.label: negative
cases.property: no comment references a post that does not exist (no orphan)
cases.environment: addComment concurrent with deletePost of the same post, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: comments.post_id REFERENCES posts(id). The existence check is redundant. If the INSERT comes after the DELETE of the post, its foreign-key check waits for or sees the deletion and fails with 23503. If the INSERT commits first, the post DELETE fails its NO ACTION check with 23503 and deletePost rolls back. Either a call fails or no orphan exists.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: no bookmark references a post that does not exist (no orphan)
cases.environment: addBookmark concurrent with deletePost of the same post, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: bookmarks.post_id is a plain column. addBookmark sees the post, deletePost then deletes the bookmarks and the post and commits, and the bookmark INSERT then succeeds, leaving an orphan.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one caller is told it holds the seat
cases.environment: two concurrent calls by different holders for one free seat, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one of the concurrent calls returns true

cases.why: Both calls read holder = NULL through the class repository, both run the unconditional UPDATE, and both return true. The table ends with a single holder (the last writer), so no table-level invariant is violated; only the return values show it.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one caller is told it holds the seat
cases.environment: two concurrent calls by different holders for one free seat, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one of the concurrent calls returns true

cases.why: UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND holder IS NULL RETURNING. The second UPDATE waits for the first row lock. Under READ COMMITTED it then re-evaluates the WHERE on the new row version, matches 0 rows and returns false. (Under REPEATABLE READ it fails with 40001, which is also not a success.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one caller is told it holds the seat
cases.environment: two calls by different holders for one seat, concurrent or one after the other, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one of the calls returns true

cases.why: UPDATE ... RETURNING without a condition on holder returns the row to both callers, so both return true. The table ends with one holder, so the violation shows only in the return values.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one order per cart (declared one-order-per-cart)
cases.environment: the process crashes after the single INSERT committed and before the response is sent; the client resubmits the same request (declared retry on-crash)
cases.why: The INSERT is the handler's final statement and the order id is database-generated. The resubmission inserts a second order for the same cart and nothing collides.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one order per cart (declared)
cases.environment: the process crashes after the INSERT committed and before the response; the client resubmits the same request with the same checkout id (declared retry on-crash)
cases.why: The client's checkout id is the primary key, written with ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING. The resubmission inserts nothing and returns the existing order id.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one payment per order (declared one-payment-per-order)
cases.environment: the first transaction commits but its COMMIT acknowledgment is lost (the driver throws); the higher-order wrapper withRetry runs the callback again
cases.why: The retried transaction inserts a second payment with a new serial id; nothing collides.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one payment per order (declared)
cases.environment: the order is pending; the first transaction commits but its COMMIT acknowledgment is lost; withRetry runs the callback again
cases.why: The retry's conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending' RETURNING matches 0 rows, so no second payment is inserted. (The retry returns false although the order was paid; this misleading response is not the labeled property.)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: read-your-writes: the returned name is the name this call wrote
cases.environment: a single call, with no concurrent rename; the replica has not yet replayed the UPDATE

observable.description: the returned name equals the name argument

cases.why: The UPDATE commits on the primary and the select is routed to the replica, which can still return the old name.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: read-your-writes: the returned name is the name this call wrote
cases.environment: a single call, with no concurrent rename; the replica lags

observable.description: the returned name equals the name argument

cases.why: The read goes through $primary, after the autocommitted UPDATE.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: read-your-writes: the returned name is the name this call wrote
cases.environment: a single call, with no concurrent rename; the replica lags

observable.description: the returned name equals the name argument

replicas.routing: transaction -> primary (tx.select runs in the primary transaction)

cases.why: withReplicas routes transaction() to the primary. The select runs inside the same transaction as the UPDATE and sees it.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one label per (team, name)
cases.environment: two SEQUENTIAL calls with the same team and name (the second starts after the first returned); the replica has not yet replayed the first INSERT
cases.why: A check-then-act whose check reads the lagging replica. It duplicates even without any concurrency, and there is no unique constraint on labels.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one team per owner (declared)
cases.environment: two concurrent requests by the same signed-in user, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: A callback wrapped by withAuth, with zod-validated input. The repository check, then INSERT, is unprotected, as in E01; the owner is the session user.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one invite per (team, email) (and at most one caller is told invited)
cases.environment: two concurrent requests for the same team and email (the email possibly differing in case or surrounding spaces), READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one request returns invited: true

cases.why: A callback wrapped by withAuth. zod trims and lowercases the email before the write. UNIQUE(team_id, email) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: the second INSERT waits for the first and then inserts nothing, and RETURNING gives it no row.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: hits equals the number of completed calls (no lost increment), at most one row per path
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same path, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: A single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (path) DO UPDATE SET hits = hits + 1. The database serializes the conflicting rows, and the increment is computed from the latest row version.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one caller is told it reserved the handle
cases.environment: two calls by different users for one free handle, concurrent or one after the other, READ COMMITTED

observable.description: at most one call returns reserved: true

cases.why: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING also returns the existing (updated) row to the second caller, so both see rows.length > 0. The table keeps one row owned by the first user.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one welcome notification per user (declared one-welcome-per-user)
cases.environment: the job is delivered at least once (declared): the worker crashes after the INSERT and before acknowledging, and the queue redelivers
cases.why: Two autocommitted statements with no deduplication. The redelivered job inserts a second notification with a new generated id.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one welcome notification per user (declared)
cases.environment: the job is delivered at least once (declared), including a crash before the acknowledgment and overlapping deliveries, READ COMMITTED
cases.why: The job id is inserted into processed_jobs (primary key, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) in the same transaction as the notification. A redelivery after the commit inserts nothing and returns. An overlapping delivery waits on the uncommitted key, then does nothing. A crash before the commit rolls everything back.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one folder per (owner, parent, name), root included
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same owner and name at the root (parentId = null), READ COMMITTED
cases.why: UNIQUE(owner_id, parent_id, name) is NULLS DISTINCT, the PostgreSQL and Drizzle default. Two rows with parent_id NULL do not conflict, so both INSERTs succeed after both checks see none. (With a non-null parent the second INSERT fails with 23505 instead.)

cases.label: unsupported
cases.why: db.execute(sql.raw(statement)): the SQL text is a runtime argument.
